proposals.evidence: DEDR5152 explicitly records Brahui hēṭ she-goat alongside Kurux ēṛā and Malto éṛe. Zoller p.743 instead relates hēṭ to OIA eḍa2512 with spontaneous aspiration, while noting a vowel difficulty; DEDR also compares Sanskrit eḍa without asserting a donor direction. This is a qualified proposal following the explicit Dravidian family placement, retaining the competing Indo-Aryan interpretation for review. This family identification does not endorse broader cross-family ancestry claims in the source.

records.Etymology: 1670. Chin. huḍ ‘ewe’ and Paṭṭ. huṛ ‘ram, male sheep’ < OIA eḍa- ‘a kind of sheep’ (2512) (Pa., Pk.) with modern reflexes in the northwest, in S. and Si. Spontaneous aspiration also in Niya Prakrit heḍˈi ‘sheep(?)’ and in Brah. hēṭ ‘she-goat’. But the vowel is unclear. Note that the lemma with initial aspiration has also been borrowed into Psht. heṛə́y ‘sheep with a long tail’ (Cheung [2013: 626, fn. 37]).

proposals.evidence: DEDR4191 explicitly records Brahui prishk spark alongside Pengo pṛiski, Manda pṛihe/pṛihki and Kuwi pṛiska/pṛisi. Zoller p.792 prints priśk spark and says it is difficult to connect with his wider Indo-Aryan spark group. The dictionary’s sh and source ś are retained as transcription variants; the exact Brahui family attestation supports4191 without endorsing the separate regional comparison. This family identification does not endorse broader cross-family ancestry claims in the source.

records.Etymology: 40. Pal. keriˈšpīka ‘spark’; Kal. kuluspík (also kulušpík, kulišpík) ‘sparks, flying ember’; Dm. kiliˈṣpik; Pr. anig išpīg ‘spark’ are probably compounds with first element re- lated with the ‘(char)coal’ words discussed p. 768 sub Jaun. kuluṇɔ ‘to singe’ (except Pr. which reflects agní- ‘fire’); second element is probably cognate with Sak. ṣpargga- ‘noise, twang’ which reflects PIE *spr̥ə̑-g- ‘crackle, sputter’. These old compounds thus appear to have an original meaning like ‘live coal spatter’. They must not necessarily be Iranian borrowings. Notes: (a) Similar looking OIA sphuliṅga- ‘spark’ is not a cognate of the above forms. In KEWA Mayrhofer quotes Burrow who suggests relation with PIE *spr̥ə̑-g-; he rightly does not repeat this suggestion in EWA. This sphuliṅga- is part of a complex and not very transparent word field with elements of Indo-Aryan and Austro-Asiatic roots. In Zoller (2018: 337ff.) I have attempted to disentangle this complex. (b) Partly similar Brah. prišk ‘spark’ and Orm. spōx ‘live coal’ are difficult to connect here.
